summary: Berray Mountain's 1965 R-6 flattop tower, its 1931 and 1940 predecessors, and a 2026 Forest Service note that restoration is underway; the trail is public, the tower is not described as open.

facts.design: R-6 flattop cab with catwalk on a 30-ft timber tower (built 1965); earlier 1940 50-ft pole tower with L-4 cab

access.note: Reached by the public Berray Mountain Trail #967 from the trailhead on Kootenai National Forest land; the trail is open and motor vehicles are barred. The sources do not say the tower is open to climbing, and restoration work is underway.

visit.trail_note: Trail #967 is Trail Class 3 and leads to the lookout; no motorized vehicles; check with the Cabinet Ranger Station for current trail conditions

facts.agency: U.S. Forest Service, Kootenai National Forest (Cabinet Ranger District, cooperator)

events.note: Crow's nest tower with a log cabin and porch for living quarters; first used about 1931 with a 20-ft observation platform
Replaced by a 50-ft pole tower with an L-4 cab
Present R-6 flattop cab on a 30-ft timber tower
Remained staffed for fire detection until 1973 per the Forest Service; other sources say regularly staffed into the early 1970s
Registered on the National Historic Lookout Register August 20, 1996
Kootenai National Forest news release dated August 16, 2015 (as quoted on Montana lookout history page): still intact, radio repeater still functional
Forest Service page (last updated August 28, 2026) says restoration efforts are currently underway to preserve the tower

corrections.current: 2017 restored: Cabinet District installed a new roof to stop water damage
corrections.proposed: 2017 assessed, with a new roof under way as part of the pre-restoration work; the lookout has not been fully restored (Forest Service says restoration is underway in 2026)
corrections.why: The 2017 Northwest Montana Lookout Association assessment says the lookout was on the Cabinet Ranger District's short list to be restored and that a new roof was being installed to protect it from further water damage. It does not record a finished restoration, and the Forest Service in 2026 still describes restoration as underway. The PDF text extracts with duplicated lines, so its wording was checked by hand rather than by quote.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: NHLR gives 6,063 ft (1,848 m); firelookout.com and the Forest Service trailhead page give 6,177 ft. The record keeps the NHLR figure (elevation_m 1848.0); the story avoids a specific number.

The Forest Service says the lookout was staffed for fire detection until 1973; firelookout.com says it was regularly staffed in the 1960s and early 1970s. The story uses the Forest Service date and notes the regular staffing from the other source.

notes_for_editor: Built dates 1931, 1940 and 1965 agree across NHLR, firelookout.com and the Weebly history. The 2017 PDF's roof and assessment lines are not quotable: pdftotext duplicates every line, so check_quotes cannot match them, and the story leaves them out. Current tower condition rests on one Forest Service sentence about restoration. The brief's 2017 'restored' event is overstated (see corrections). Elevation disagrees by about 114 ft between sources. Trail access is public; nothing supports climbing the tower and the story says so.
